chapter: Ch 4 — Mathematics of Finance (Time Value of Money)

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Time value of money · Concept
questions.stem: A supplier offers Ashwin either ₹ 1,00,000 today or ₹ 1,00,000 one year from today, with no risk of default in either case. Ashwin prefers the money today. The BEST reason is:

options.text: Money received today can be invested and will grow to more than ₹ 1,00,000 in a year
options.explanation: Correct. The earning capacity of money is the reason a rupee today outranks a rupee later. Even with default risk removed, today's ₹ 1,00,000 placed at any positive rate becomes more than ₹ 1,00,000 by next year, so the two sums are not equivalent.

options.text: ₹ 1,00,000 today is a larger number of rupees than ₹ 1,00,000 next year
options.explanation: The two sums carry the same number of rupees. What differs is the date they arrive, and the interest that date makes possible.

options.text: The supplier may fail to pay next year
options.explanation: A real reason in practice, but the question expressly removes default risk. The preference survives even so, which is the point of the time value of money.

options.text: Interest rates are expected to fall during the year
options.explanation: The preference holds at any positive rate, rising or falling. No forecast about rates is needed.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Simple and compound interest · Concept
questions.stem: For the same principal, the same rate and the same period, simple interest and compound interest are EQUAL when:

options.text: The rate of interest is below 10% per annum
options.explanation: The size of the rate does not matter. Interest on interest arises at every positive rate once a second period begins.

options.text: The period is exactly one conversion period
options.explanation: Correct. In the first period there is no accumulated interest to earn interest on, so both methods charge P i. From the second period onward the compound figure is always the larger.
Both formulas are proportional to the principal, so the size of P never changes which method gives more.

options.text: Interest is compounded quarterly rather than yearly
options.explanation: More frequent compounding widens the gap rather than closing it, because interest starts earning sooner.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Rate and time · Concept
questions.stem: A deposit runs for 3 years at 10% per annum compounded half-yearly. The values of i and n to be substituted in A = P(1 + i)^n are:

options.explanation: This ignores the conversion period altogether and treats half-yearly compounding as yearly, understating the amount.
The number of periods has been doubled but the rate has not been halved, so each half-year is charged a full year's rate. Rate and time must be adjusted together.
The rate has been halved but the periods have not been doubled, so half the interest disappears.
Correct. Half-yearly conversion means m = 2, so i = 0.10 ÷ 2 = 0.05 per half-year and n = 3 × 2 = 6 half-years. Both adjustments are made together, and the rate is used as a decimal.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Simple interest · Interest and amount
questions.stem: ₹ 75,000 is lent for 4 years at 8.5% per annum simple interest. The interest is:

options.explanation: This compounds the interest yearly — 75,000[(1.085)^4 − 1]. The question says simple interest, so interest never joins the principal.
This is the amount, P + I = 75,000 + 25,500. The question asks for the interest alone.
Correct. I = P i t = 75,000 × 0.085 × 4 = ₹ 25,500. Every year adds the same ₹ 6,375 because simple interest is always charged on the original principal.
This is one year's interest. The loan runs for four years, so multiply by t.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Simple interest · Solving for the principal
questions.stem: A sum lent at 9% per annum simple interest earned ₹ 18,900 in 3 years and 6 months. The sum lent was:

options.explanation: Correct. P = I ÷ (i t) = 18,900 ÷ (0.09 × 3.5) = 18,900 ÷ 0.315 = ₹ 60,000. Six months is treated as an exact half-year, so t = 3.5.
This drops the six months and uses t = 3, so the divisor is 0.27 instead of 0.315. Part years must be carried as exact twelfths.
This is the amount at maturity, 60,000 + 18,900. The question asks for the sum lent.
This leaves the rate as 9 instead of 0.09, so the answer comes out a hundred times too small.

questions.stem: ₹ 2,40,000 is deposited for 146 days at 7.5% per annum simple interest. Taking a year as 365 days, the interest is:

options.explanation: This uses a 360-day year: 2,40,000 × 0.075 × 146 ÷ 360. The question fixes the year at 365 days.
This charges a full year's interest and ignores the 146-day period.
This is the amount repayable, not the interest.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Simple interest · Solving for the rate
questions.stem: A sum of money doubles itself in 12 years and 6 months under simple interest. The rate per annum is:

options.explanation: This doubles the correct rate. Doubling means the interest EQUALS the principal, so i t = 1, not 2.
This applies the rule of 72 (72 ÷ 12.5), which approximates a COMPOUND doubling time. Under simple interest the exact relation i = 1 ÷ t applies.
Correct. Doubling means I = P, so P = P i t gives i = 1 ÷ t = 1 ÷ 12.5 = 0.08, that is 8% per annum. The principal cancels, so it never needed to be known.
This quotes the time as if it were the rate. The two are reciprocals here, not equal.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Simple interest · A rate that changes
questions.stem: ₹ 90,000 is lent at 6% per annum simple interest for the first 2 years and 9% per annum for the next 3 years. The total interest is:

options.explanation: This compounds each slice — 90,000 × (1.06)² × (1.09)³ − 90,000. Simple interest never adds interest to the principal.
This averages the two rates to 7.5% and runs it for all 5 years. The rates apply for unequal periods, so a plain average is not the same as the correct slice-by-slice total.
This adds the two rates to 15% and applies the total for the whole 5 years, counting both rates in every year.
Correct. Each slice is worked on the same original principal: 90,000 × 0.06 × 2 = ₹ 10,800, plus 90,000 × 0.09 × 3 = ₹ 24,300, giving ₹ 35,100.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Simple interest · Time in months
questions.stem: ₹ 1,50,000 is borrowed for 8 months at 11% per annum simple interest. The interest payable is:

options.explanation: Correct. Eight months is 8/12 of a year, so I = 1,50,000 × 0.11 × 8 ÷ 12 = ₹ 11,000.
This charges a full year's interest and ignores that the loan runs for only eight months.
This reads the 8 months as 8 years. The rate is per annum, so the time must be converted into years before it is used.
This is the amount repayable, ₹ 1,50,000 + ₹ 11,000, not the interest.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Simple interest · Solving for the time
questions.stem: In how many years will ₹ 50,000 amount to ₹ 68,000 at 9% per annum simple interest?

options.explanation: This uses the AMOUNT of ₹ 68,000 as if it were the interest. The interest is 68,000 − 50,000 = ₹ 18,000.
This is the answer under COMPOUND interest, log 1.36 ÷ log 1.09. Compounding reaches the target sooner, but the question says simple interest.
This halves the correct answer, as though the interest were ₹ 9,000 rather than ₹ 18,000.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Compound interest · Interest for three years
questions.stem: ₹ 1,80,000 is invested for 3 years at 7% per annum compounded yearly. The compound interest is:

options.explanation: This is the AMOUNT at maturity. Compound interest is the amount minus the principal.
This is simple interest, 1,80,000 × 0.07 × 3. It ignores the interest earned on interest in years 2 and 3.
This compounds half-yearly at 3.5% for 6 periods. The question says the conversion is yearly, so i = 0.07 and n = 3.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Compound interest · Difference over two years
questions.stem: On ₹ 2,50,000 at 8% per annum for 2 years, the difference between compound interest (yearly conversion) and simple interest is:

options.explanation: This is one year's interest, P i. The difference between the two methods is P i², a much smaller figure.
This is the compound interest itself, 2,50,000[(1.08)² − 1]. The question asks by how much it EXCEEDS the simple interest.
This is the simple interest, 2,50,000 × 0.08 × 2 — the other half of the comparison, not the difference.

Correct. Compound interest ₹ 41,600 less simple interest ₹ 40,000 = ₹ 1,600. The two-year shortcut gives the same: P i² = 2,50,000 × 0.0064 = ₹ 1,600, which is simply the second year's interest on the first year's interest.

readLink.label: Read: Compound interest, §3 →

questions.sourceRef: Two-year difference between CI and SI = P i²

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Compound interest · Difference over three years
questions.stem: On ₹ 1,00,000 at 10% per annum for 3 years, compound interest (yearly conversion) exceeds simple interest by:

options.explanation: Correct. Compound interest = 1,00,000[(1.10)³ − 1] = ₹ 33,100; simple interest = ₹ 30,000; the excess is ₹ 3,100. The three-year shortcut P i²(3 + i) = 1,00,000 × 0.01 × 3.10 gives the same figure.
This applies the TWO-year shortcut P i². For three years the multiplier is (3 + i), not 1.
This is the compound interest itself, not the excess over simple interest.
This is the simple interest for three years, not the difference between the two methods.

readLink.label: Read: Compound interest, §3 →

questions.sourceRef: Three-year difference between CI and SI = P i²(3 + i)

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Compound interest · Working back to the principal
questions.stem: The difference between compound interest (yearly conversion) and simple interest on a certain sum for 2 years at 12% per annum is ₹ 4,320. The sum is:

options.explanation: This divides by i instead of by i², that is 4,320 ÷ 0.12. The two-year difference is P i², so the divisor is 0.0144.
Correct. The two-year difference is P i², so P = 4,320 ÷ (0.12)² = 4,320 ÷ 0.0144 = ₹ 3,00,000. Check: compound interest ₹ 76,320 less simple interest ₹ 72,000 = ₹ 4,320.
This uses 0.144 in place of 0.0144 — a one-place decimal slip in squaring the rate.
This applies the THREE-year difference formula P i²(3 + i) to a two-year question, dividing by an extra factor of 3.12.

readLink.label: Read: Compound interest, §3 →

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Compound decay · Constant rate of decline
questions.stem: A machine costing ₹ 9,60,000 loses 12% of its written-down value every year. Its value at the end of 4 years is:

options.explanation: This takes 12% of the ORIGINAL cost every year (₹ 1,15,200 × 4). The question says the decline is on the written-down value, so the base shrinks each year.
This is the total fall in value over the four years, not the value that remains.
Correct. Value = P(1 − d)^n = 9,60,000 × (0.88)^4 = 9,60,000 × 0.599695 = ₹ 5,75,707.55. Each year multiplies the previous balance by 0.88.
This compounds the value upward at 12%, using (1.12)^4 instead of (0.88)^4. A declining rate enters the formula as (1 − d).

questions.sourceRef: Value after n periods = P(1 − d)^n

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Compound interest · Rate changing mid-term
questions.stem: ₹ 4,00,000 is invested for 2 years at 6% per annum and then for 3 more years at 9% per annum, compounded yearly throughout. The amount at the end of 5 years is:

options.explanation: This charges simple interest on each slice, 4,00,000 × 0.06 × 2 plus 4,00,000 × 0.09 × 3, added to the principal. The question says the interest is compounded.
This averages the two rates to 7.5% and compounds for five years. The rates run for unequal periods, so their factors must be multiplied, not averaged.
This is the compound interest earned, not the amount. Add the principal back.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Compound interest · Working back to the principal
questions.stem: A sum invested at 10% per annum compounded yearly amounts to ₹ 1,33,100 after 3 years. The sum invested was:

options.explanation: This divides by (1 + i t) = 1.30, which is the SIMPLE interest amount factor. Compounding needs (1.10)³ = 1.331.
This deducts 10% for each of the three years as a flat 30% of the maturity amount. Discounting divides by 1.331; it never subtracts a percentage.
This multiplies by 1.331 instead of dividing, pushing the sum three years further forward instead of pulling it back.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Conversion periods · Quarterly compounding
questions.stem: ₹ 1,60,000 is deposited for 3 years at 10% per annum compounded quarterly. The maturity amount is:

options.explanation: This compounds yearly at 10% for 3 years and ignores the quarterly conversion, so interest starts earning later than it should.
This multiplies the periods by 4 but leaves the rate at 10% per period, charging a full year's rate every quarter.
This divides the rate by 4 but leaves n at 3, so only three quarters of interest are counted instead of twelve.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Conversion periods · Monthly compounding
questions.stem: ₹ 3,00,000 is placed for 2 years at 9% per annum compounded monthly. The amount at the end is:

options.explanation: This compounds yearly at 9% for two years and ignores the monthly conversion period.
This uses 24 periods but keeps the rate at 9% for each MONTH, charging twelve times the intended interest.
This divides the rate by 12 but leaves n at 2, counting only two months of interest instead of twenty-four.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Conversion periods · Frequency of compounding
questions.stem: ₹ 1,00,000 is invested for one year at a nominal 12% per annum. Which conversion period gives the LARGEST amount at the end of the year?

options.explanation: Yearly conversion adds interest only once, at the very end, so it is always the smallest of the four.
Better than yearly, because the first half-year's ₹ 6,000 earns for six months, but two conversions are still fewer than four or twelve.
Larger than half-yearly for the same reason, but monthly conversion adds interest eight more times in the year.

Correct. 1,00,000 × (1.01)^12 = ₹ 1,12,682.50. For a given nominal rate, the more often interest is converted, the larger the amount, because each conversion lets interest begin earning sooner. The gains shrink as the frequency rises and approach a ceiling at continuous compounding.

readLink.label: Read: Nominal rate, effective rate and continuous compounding, §6 →

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Conversion periods · Half-yearly compounding
questions.stem: ₹ 2,00,000 is invested for 4 years and 6 months at 8% per annum compounded half-yearly. The amount is:

options.explanation: This halves the rate but leaves n at 4.5 years, so only about half the conversion periods are counted.
This uses 9 periods at the full 8%, charging a whole year's rate in every half-year.
This compounds yearly at 8% for 4.5 years and ignores the half-yearly conversion. It is close to the right answer, which is exactly why the conversion period must be handled deliberately.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Solving for the rate
questions.stem: ₹ 1,50,000 invested for 6 years, compounded yearly, grew to ₹ 2,50,000. The rate of interest per annum is approximately:

options.explanation: This is the SIMPLE interest rate, ₹ 1,00,000 ÷ (1,50,000 × 6). Compounding reaches the same total with a lower yearly rate.
This is the total growth over the whole six years, not a rate per annum.
This takes the sixth root correctly but forgets to subtract 1. The root gives the growth FACTOR of 1.0889; the rate is what is left after removing the original 1.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Solving for the time · Doubling
questions.stem: In how many years will ₹ 80,000 double itself at 7% per annum compounded yearly? Take log 2 = 0.3010 and log 1.07 = 0.0294.

options.explanation: This is the SIMPLE interest answer, 1 ÷ 0.07. Compounding doubles the money sooner because interest earns interest.
Correct. (1.07)^n = 2, so n = log 2 ÷ log 1.07 = 0.3010 ÷ 0.0294 = 10.24 years. The principal of ₹ 80,000 never enters the working — only the ratio A ÷ P does.
This is the rule-of-72 approximation, 72 ÷ 7. It is a useful check but not the exact answer the logs give.
This doubles the correct answer, as though doubling the money needed twice the doubling time.

readLink.label: Read: Solving for the rate and for the time, §5 →

questions.sourceRef: n = log(A ÷ P) ÷ log(1 + i)

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Solving for the time · Reaching a target
questions.stem: How long will ₹ 5,00,000 take to reach ₹ 9,00,000 at 8% per annum compounded yearly? Take log 1.8 = 0.2553 and log 1.08 = 0.0334.

options.explanation: This is the simple interest answer: ₹ 4,00,000 of interest ÷ (5,00,000 × 0.08). Compounding gets there faster.
This divides the ratio 1.8 by the rate 0.08. The ratio must be divided in LOGARITHMS: log 1.8 ÷ log 1.08.
This is the rule of 72 (72 ÷ 8), which estimates the time to DOUBLE. The target here is 1.8 times, not 2 times.

readLink.label: Read: Solving for the rate and for the time, §5 →

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Compound interest · Multiples and powers
questions.stem: A sum of money becomes 3 times itself in 15 years at compound interest. In how many years will the same sum become 9 times itself at the same rate?

options.explanation: This multiplies the 15 years by 9. Growth is multiplicative, so the multiple 9 relates to 3 as a POWER, not as a multiplier of time.
This treats 9 as one and a half times as far along as 3 and scales the years by 1.5. That would be right for simple interest, not for compounding.
This multiplies the 15 years by 3, the usual proportional reasoning. It would suit simple interest, where equal amounts of interest accrue each year.
Correct. (1 + i)^15 = 3, and 9 = 3², so (1 + i)^30 = 3² = 9. Tripling twice takes twice as long, giving 30 years.

readLink.label: Read: Solving for the rate and for the time, §5 →

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Effective rate of interest
questions.stem: The effective annual rate corresponding to a nominal 12% per annum compounded quarterly is:

options.explanation: This is the NOMINAL rate as advertised. The effective rate exceeds it whenever conversion happens more than once a year.
This is the effective rate for HALF-YEARLY conversion, (1.06)² − 1. Quarterly conversion compounds twice as often.
This is the rate per quarter, not the effective rate for the year.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Effective rate · Comparing two offers
questions.stem: Bank P offers 10% per annum compounded half-yearly. Bank Q offers 9.9% per annum compounded monthly. Which is better for a depositor, and what is the better effective annual rate?

options.explanation: Bank P's effective rate is correctly computed as (1.05)² − 1 = 10.25%, but Bank Q's monthly conversion lifts its effective rate above that, to 10.3618%.
Correct. Bank P: (1.05)² − 1 = 10.2500%. Bank Q: (1 + 0.099 ÷ 12)^12 − 1 = 10.3618%. Q wins despite its lower nominal rate, because it converts twelve times a year instead of twice.

options.text: Bank P, because 10% is higher than 9.9%
options.explanation: This compares the NOMINAL rates. Nominal rates quoted on different conversion periods are not comparable; convert both to effective rates first.
This computes Bank Q's effective rate on HALF-YEARLY conversion, (1 + 0.099 ÷ 2)² − 1. Bank Q converts monthly, so m = 12.

readLink.label: Read: Nominal rate, effective rate and continuous compounding, §6 →

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Nominal rate from an effective rate
questions.stem: A deposit scheme is to yield an effective annual rate of 8.16%, with interest converted half-yearly. The nominal rate the bank must advertise is:

options.explanation: This quotes the effective rate itself. The nominal rate must be lower, because half-yearly conversion adds something on its own.
This simply halves the effective rate. Halving is the last step in finding the periodic rate from a nominal rate, not the way back from an effective rate.
This uses m = 4 (quarterly conversion) in the same formula. The scheme converts half-yearly, so m = 2.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Continuous compounding · Amount
questions.stem: ₹ 2,50,000 is invested for 4 years at 6% per annum compounded continuously. Taking e = 2.71828, the amount is:

options.explanation: This compounds yearly, 2,50,000 × (1.06)^4. Continuous compounding gives a little more, because interest is converted at every instant.
This is the simple-interest amount, 2,50,000 × (1 + 0.06 × 4).
This uses e^0.06 only, dropping the time from the exponent. The exponent is r × t, not r alone.

readLink.label: Read: Nominal rate, effective rate and continuous compounding, §6 →

questions.sourceRef: A = P e^(r t)

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Continuous compounding · Effective rate
questions.stem: The effective annual rate of interest corresponding to a nominal 10% per annum compounded continuously is:

options.explanation: This is the nominal rate. Continuous conversion always lifts the effective rate above it.
This is the effective rate for MONTHLY conversion, (1 + 0.10 ÷ 12)^12 − 1. Continuous conversion is the limit beyond that, and gives a shade more.
This subtracts nothing and misreads e itself as a rate. The formula is e^r − 1, with r = 0.10, not e − 1.
Correct. E = e^r − 1 = e^0.10 − 1 = 1.105171 − 1 = 0.105171, that is 10.5171%. This is the ceiling that no finite conversion frequency can pass at a 10% nominal rate.

readLink.label: Read: Nominal rate, effective rate and continuous compounding, §6 →

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Present value of a single sum
questions.stem: What is the present value of ₹ 6,00,000 receivable at the end of 5 years, if money is worth 11% per annum compounded yearly?

options.explanation: Correct. PV = FV(1 + i)^(−n) = 6,00,000 × (1.11)^(−5) = 6,00,000 × 0.593451 = ₹ 3,56,070.80. That sum invested today at 11% would itself grow to ₹ 6,00,000 in five years.
This multiplies by (1.11)^5 instead of dividing, pushing the sum five years further into the future instead of pulling it back to today.
This discounts on a SIMPLE interest basis, dividing by (1 + i t) = 1.55. The question compounds, so the divisor is (1.11)^5 = 1.685058.
This deducts 11% for each of the five years as a flat 55% of the future sum. Discounting divides by a factor; it does not subtract a percentage.

readLink.label: Read: Present value and future value of a single sum, §7 →

questions.sourceRef: PV = FV(1 + i)^(−n)

questions.stem: A contract will pay ₹ 2,00,000 at the end of year 1, ₹ 2,50,000 at the end of year 2 and ₹ 1,80,000 at the end of year 3. At a discount rate of 9% per annum, the contract is worth today:

options.explanation: This is the face value of the three receipts added up, with no discounting at all. Rupees arriving on different dates cannot simply be added.
This applies the three-year annuity factor 2.531295 to the average receipt of ₹ 2,10,000. Annuity factors work only when every payment is the same.
This discounts every flow by three years, as though all three arrived at the end of year 3. Each flow carries the factor for its own year.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Annuity · Solving for the deposit
questions.stem: What sum must be deposited at the end of each year for 10 years, at 7% per annum compounded yearly, to accumulate ₹ 20,00,000?

options.explanation: This divides the target by 10 and ignores the interest the earlier deposits earn. The deposits must be smaller than that.
Correct. R = S i ÷ [(1 + i)^n − 1] = 20,00,000 ÷ 13.816448 = ₹ 1,44,755.01. Ten such deposits total ₹ 14,47,550, and interest supplies the remaining ₹ 5,52,450.
This divides by the PRESENT value annuity factor 7.023582. A target at a FUTURE date needs the future value factor, which is always larger.
This treats the deposits as being made at the beginning of each year, dividing further by 1.07. The question says they fall at the end.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Present value of an ordinary annuity
questions.stem: A contract will pay ₹ 75,000 at the end of each year for 8 years. At 12% per annum, its present value is:

options.explanation: This adds the eight payments at face value. Payments spread over eight years are worth less than their total today.
This uses the FUTURE value annuity factor 12.299693, which values the stream at the END of year 8, not today.

Correct. P(8, 12%) = [1 − (1.12)^(−8)] ÷ 0.12 = 4.967640, so the present value is 75,000 × 4.967640 = ₹ 3,72,572.98. Note the factor 4.97 is below the 8 payments, as a present value factor always must be.
This multiplies by 1.12 as though the payments came at the beginning of each year. The question says they come at the end.

readLink.label: Read: Present value of an ordinary annuity, §10 →

questions.sourceRef: PV of an ordinary annuity = R[1 − (1 + i)^(−n)] ÷ i

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Annuity · Solving for the withdrawal
questions.stem: ₹ 12,00,000 is invested today at 10% per annum compounded yearly, and is to be drawn down by 5 equal withdrawals at the end of each of the next 5 years, leaving nothing at the end. Each withdrawal is:

options.explanation: This divides the fund by 5 and ignores the interest the unwithdrawn balance keeps earning, so it understates each withdrawal.
This divides by the FUTURE value annuity factor 6.105100. The fund exists today, so the present value factor is the right divisor.
This assumes the withdrawals are taken at the BEGINNING of each year, dividing further by 1.10. Withdrawing earlier would mean smaller withdrawals, but the question says they fall at the end.
Correct. R = PV ÷ P(5, 10%) = 12,00,000 ÷ 3.790787 = ₹ 3,16,556.98. The five withdrawals total ₹ 15,82,784.85, the excess over ₹ 12,00,000 being the interest earned along the way.

readLink.label: Read: Present value of an ordinary annuity, §10 →

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Annuity due · Future value
questions.stem: ₹ 20,000 is deposited at the BEGINNING of each year for 7 years into a fund earning 9% per annum compounded yearly. The fund at the end of 7 years is:

options.explanation: This is the ordinary annuity answer, 20,000 × 9.200435. Deposits made at the beginning of each year each earn one extra year of interest, so the result must be multiplied by 1.09.
This adds the seven deposits and credits no interest at all.
Correct. A(7, 9%) = 9.200435, so the ordinary annuity value is ₹ 1,84,008.69; multiplying by (1 + i) = 1.09 for the annuity due gives ₹ 2,00,569.48.
This uses the present value annuity factor 5.032953, valuing the deposits today instead of at the end of year 7.

readLink.label: Read: Annuity due, §11 →

questions.sourceRef: FV of an annuity due = R[(1 + i)^n − 1] ÷ i × (1 + i)

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Annuity due · Present value
questions.stem: A godown is taken on rent for 6 years at ₹ 1,80,000 a year, payable in ADVANCE at the start of each year. At 10% per annum, the present value of the rent is:

options.explanation: Correct. P(6, 10%) = 4.355261, so the ordinary annuity value is ₹ 7,83,946.93; rent paid in advance is an annuity due, so multiply by 1.10 to get ₹ 8,62,341.62.
This treats the rent as payable at the END of each year. Payment in advance shifts every instalment one year earlier and raises the present value by a factor of 1.10.
This adds six years of rent at face value, with no discounting.
This uses the future value annuity factor 7.715610, valuing the rent at the end of year 6 instead of today.

readLink.label: Read: Annuity due, §11 →

questions.sourceRef: PV of an annuity due = R[1 − (1 + i)^(−n)] ÷ i × (1 + i)

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Perpetuity
questions.stem: A trust wishes to pay a prize of ₹ 60,000 at the end of every year for ever. If the fund earns 8% per annum, the sum that must be endowed today is:

options.explanation: This divides by 8 instead of by 0.08, leaving the rate as a whole number instead of a decimal.
Correct. PV of a perpetuity = R ÷ i = 60,000 ÷ 0.08 = ₹ 7,50,000. The fund itself is never spent; its yearly interest of ₹ 60,000 pays the prize for ever.
This multiplies the prize by the rate instead of dividing by it, giving the interest on ₹ 60,000 rather than the capital that produces ₹ 60,000.
This values only the first 20 years of prizes, using P(20, 8%) = 9.818147. A perpetuity never stops, so the annuity factor must be taken to its limit, 1 ÷ i.

readLink.label: Read: Perpetuity and growing perpetuity, §12 →

questions.sourceRef: PV of a perpetuity = R ÷ i

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Growing perpetuity
questions.stem: A scholarship of ₹ 90,000 is to be paid at the end of next year and is to grow by 5% every year thereafter, for ever. If the endowment fund earns 11% per annum, the capital required today is:

options.explanation: This treats the scholarship as level, dividing by 0.11 alone. A payment that grows needs a smaller net discount rate and therefore more capital.
This divides by the growth rate g = 0.05 instead of by (i − g). Growth alone cannot discount anything.
This grows the numerator once more, using ₹ 94,500. The ₹ 90,000 given is already the payment one year from now, which is exactly what the formula needs.
Correct. PV = R ÷ (i − g) = 90,000 ÷ (0.11 − 0.05) = 90,000 ÷ 0.06 = ₹ 15,00,000. The formula holds because g = 5% is below i = 11%.

readLink.label: Read: Perpetuity and growing perpetuity, §12 →

questions.sourceRef: PV of a growing perpetuity = R ÷ (i − g)

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Sinking fund
questions.stem: A company must repay ₹ 25,00,000 of debentures at the end of 5 years. It will make equal deposits at the end of each year into a sinking fund earning 10% per annum compounded yearly. The yearly deposit is:

options.explanation: Correct. R = S i ÷ [(1 + i)^n − 1] = 25,00,000 ÷ 6.105100 = ₹ 4,09,493.70. Five deposits total ₹ 20,47,468.51 and the fund's own interest supplies the remaining ₹ 4,52,531.49.
This divides the target by 5 and credits the fund with no interest.
This divides by the present value annuity factor 3.790787. The target sits at a future date, so the future value annuity factor is the right divisor.
This assumes the deposits are made at the beginning of each year, dividing further by 1.10. The question says they fall at the end.

readLink.label: Read: Sinking funds, §13 →

questions.sourceRef: Sinking fund deposit R = S i ÷ [(1 + i)^n − 1]

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Loan amortisation · Equated monthly instalment
questions.stem: A loan of ₹ 6,00,000 is taken at 12% per annum compounded monthly, repayable in 36 equal monthly instalments beginning one month after the loan. The instalment is:

options.explanation: This repays only the principal, ₹ 6,00,000 ÷ 36, and charges no interest.
This is the flat-rate method: total simple interest of ₹ 2,16,000 added to the principal and divided by 36. It overcharges, because it ignores that the outstanding balance falls every month.
This treats the instalments as payable at the BEGINNING of each month, dividing further by 1.01. The first instalment falls one month after the loan, so this is an ordinary annuity.

readLink.label: Read: Loan amortisation and the equated instalment, §14 →

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Loan amortisation · Balance outstanding
questions.stem: A loan of ₹ 10,00,000 at 11% per annum is repayable in 6 equal yearly instalments, the first one year from the loan. The amount still outstanding immediately after the fourth instalment is:

options.explanation: This assumes the principal is repaid evenly, two-sixths of ₹ 10,00,000 remaining. Early instalments are mostly interest, so more principal than that is still outstanding.
This adds the two remaining instalments at face value. The balance owed today is their PRESENT value, which is smaller.
This multiplies the correct balance by 1.11, as though the two remaining instalments fell at the beginning of each year rather than the end.

readLink.label: Read: Loan amortisation and the equated instalment, §14 →

questions.sourceRef: Balance after k instalments = R × P(n − k, i)

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Net present value
questions.stem: A project costs ₹ 15,00,000 today and returns ₹ 5,00,000 at the end of each of the next 4 years. At a required return of 10% per annum, its net present value is:

options.explanation: This subtracts the outlay from the undiscounted total of ₹ 20,00,000. Inflows spread over four years are worth less than their face total.
This is the present value of the inflows. The NET present value still needs the ₹ 15,00,000 outlay deducted.
This discounts the outlay by one year as well. Money spent today carries a factor of 1 and is never discounted.
Correct. P(4, 10%) = 3.169865, so the inflows are worth 5,00,000 × 3.169865 = ₹ 15,84,932.72 and the NPV is 15,84,932.72 − 15,00,000 = ₹ 84,932.72. Positive, so the project is acceptable at 10%.

readLink.label: Read: Net present value and the accept-reject rule, §15 →

questions.sourceRef: NPV = PV of inflows − PV of outflows

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Net present value · The accept-reject rule
questions.stem: The same project — ₹ 15,00,000 today for ₹ 5,00,000 at the end of each of 4 years — is re-examined at a required return of 14% per annum. The NPV and the decision are:

options.explanation: Correct. P(4, 14%) = 2.913712, so the inflows are worth 5,00,000 × 2.913712 = ₹ 14,56,856.15 and the NPV is 14,56,856.15 − 15,00,000 = −₹ 43,143.85. A negative NPV means the project earns less than the required 14%, so it is rejected.
This is the NPV at 10%, the rate used in the earlier question. A higher required return shrinks every discount factor and can turn a positive NPV negative.
This is the present value of the inflows with the ₹ 15,00,000 outlay never deducted.

options.text: Negative ₹ 43,143.85 — accept the project, since the cash inflows exceed the outlay
options.explanation: The arithmetic is right and the rule is inverted. The inflows total ₹ 20,00,000 in face value, but that is not the test: a negative NPV means those rupees, discounted at the return the firm demands, fall short of the outlay.

readLink.label: Read: Net present value and the accept-reject rule, §15 →

questions.sourceRef: NPV decision rule; the effect of a higher discount rate

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Profitability index
questions.stem: A proposal costs ₹ 8,00,000 today and yields ₹ 2,50,000 at the end of each of the next 5 years. At 12% per annum, its profitability index is:

options.explanation: This divides the undiscounted inflows of ₹ 12,50,000 by the outlay. The profitability index uses the PRESENT value of the inflows.
Correct. P(5, 12%) = 3.604776, so the inflows are worth 2,50,000 × 3.604776 = ₹ 9,01,194.05 and PI = 9,01,194.05 ÷ 8,00,000 = 1.1265. Above 1, so the proposal is acceptable.
This inverts the ratio, dividing the outlay by the present value of the inflows. The index is benefits over cost, not cost over benefits.
This is the surplus per rupee invested, that is PI − 1. The index itself includes the rupee returned as well as the surplus, so it is 1.1265.

readLink.label: Read: Profitability index, §16 →

questions.sourceRef: PI = PV of inflows ÷ PV of the outlay

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Compound annual growth rate
questions.stem: A firm's sales rose from ₹ 40,00,000 in 2019-20 to ₹ 90,00,000 in 2025-26. The compound annual growth rate is:

options.explanation: This is a simple average: the ₹ 50,00,000 increase spread over six years as a percentage of the opening figure. It ignores that each year's growth builds on the last.
This is the total growth across the whole period, not a rate per annum.
This counts 5 years instead of 6. Count the intervals between the two years, not the year labels.

readLink.label: Read: Compound annual growth rate, §17 →

questions.sourceRef: CAGR = (Ending ÷ Beginning)^(1/n) − 1

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Bond valuation
questions.stem: A bond of face value ₹ 1,000 pays a 10% coupon at the end of each year and is redeemable at par after 4 years. Investors require a return of 8% per annum. The value of the bond today is:

options.explanation: This discounts the coupons and the redemption at the COUPON rate of 10%, which always returns the face value. Discounting uses the required yield of 8%.
This adds four coupons of ₹ 100 to the ₹ 1,000 redemption without discounting anything.
This swaps the two rates, taking an ₹ 80 coupon and discounting at 10%. The coupon rate fixes the rupee coupon; the yield does the discounting.

Correct. Value = 100 × P(4, 8%) + 1,000 × (1.08)^(−4) = 100 × 3.312127 + 1,000 × 0.735030 = 331.21 + 735.03 = ₹ 1,066.24. The bond sells at a premium because its 10% coupon beats the 8% the market requires.

readLink.label: Read: Valuing a simple bond, §18 →

questions.sourceRef: Bond value = Coupon × P(n, y) + Redemption × (1 + y)^(−n)

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Loan amortisation · Case: a twenty-year housing loan
questions.case: Meghana and Karthik have been sanctioned a housing loan of ₹ 36,00,000 by a bank in Mysuru. The rate is 9% per annum with interest compounded monthly, and the loan is repayable in 240 equal monthly instalments, the first falling due one month after disbursement. The couple wants four things settled before they sign: what the instalment will be, how much of the very first instalment is merely interest, what will still be owed after five years of paying, and what the loan will cost them in interest over its whole life. Take the monthly rate as i = 0.09 ÷ 12 = 0.0075 throughout, work from the unrounded instalment, and round only the final money figures.

readLink.label: Read: Loan amortisation and the equated instalment, §14 →

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Equated monthly instalment
questions.stem: The equated monthly instalment is:

options.explanation: This is the flat-rate method: simple interest of ₹ 64,80,000 over 20 years added to the principal and divided by 240. It ignores that the balance falls every month.
This is ₹ 36,00,000 ÷ 240, the principal alone with no interest at all.
This is the first month's interest, 36,00,000 × 0.0075. An instalment must cover the interest AND repay some principal.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Split of the first instalment
questions.stem: Of the FIRST instalment, the amount that is interest is:

options.explanation: This is the whole instalment. Part of it repays principal, so the interest is smaller.
This is the PRINCIPAL repaid in month one, the instalment less the interest. The question asks for the interest.

Correct. Interest for a period is the opening balance times the periodic rate: 36,00,000 × 0.0075 = ₹ 27,000. Only ₹ 5,390.13 of the first instalment touches the principal, which is why the balance falls so slowly at the start.
This is a full year's interest at 9% on ₹ 36,00,000. The instalment is monthly, so the periodic rate is 0.75%.

questions.sourceRef: Interest for the period = opening balance × i

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Balance outstanding
questions.stem: Immediately after the 60th instalment, the amount still owed is:

options.explanation: This assumes the principal falls evenly, leaving three-quarters after a quarter of the term. Early instalments are mostly interest, so more is owed than an even split suggests — but less than this, because 180 instalments still stand.
This adds the 180 remaining instalments at face value. The balance owed today is their PRESENT value.
This subtracts the 60 instalments paid from the loan, as though every rupee paid had reduced the principal. Most of those rupees were interest.

Correct. The balance is the present value of the instalments still to come: 180 remain, so P(180, 0.75%) = 98.593409 and the balance is 32,390.13 × 98.593409 = ₹ 31,93,453.76. After a quarter of the term, only about 11% of the principal has been repaid.

questions.sourceRef: Balance after k instalments = R × P(n − k, i)

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Total interest over the life of the loan
questions.stem: Over the full 240 months, the total interest paid is:

options.explanation: This is flat simple interest, 36,00,000 × 0.09 × 20. It charges the full rate on the whole loan for the whole term, though the balance is falling throughout.
Correct. Total paid = 240 × 32,390.13 = ₹ 77,73,632.26, of which ₹ 36,00,000 is principal, so the interest is ₹ 41,73,632.26 — more than the sum borrowed, which is what a twenty-year term does.
This is the total of all 240 instalments, principal included. Deduct the ₹ 36,00,000 borrowed to isolate the interest.
This is the principal itself, not the interest charged on it.

questions.sourceRef: Total interest = n × R − Loan

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Capital budgeting · Case: choosing between two machines
questions.case: Sahyadri Packaging Ltd can install one of two machines in the single bay it has free at its Belagavi plant. Machine A costs ₹ 20,00,000 today and is expected to bring net cash inflows of ₹ 6,00,000 at the end of each of the next 5 years. Machine B costs ₹ 24,00,000 today and is expected to bring ₹ 5,00,000, ₹ 7,00,000, ₹ 8,00,000, ₹ 9,00,000 and ₹ 6,00,000 at the ends of years 1 to 5. Neither machine has a scrap value. The company's cost of capital is 13% per annum, and the bay can hold only one machine, so the two proposals are mutually exclusive. Discount factors at 13% are 0.8850, 0.7831, 0.6931, 0.6133 and 0.5428 for years 1 to 5, and their total, the five-year annuity factor, is 3.5172.

readLink.label: Read: Net present value and the accept-reject rule, §15 →

questions.topic: Ch 4 · NPV of equal inflows
questions.stem: The net present value of Machine A is:

options.explanation: This subtracts the outlay from the undiscounted inflows of ₹ 30,00,000, ignoring that the inflows arrive over five years.
This is the present value of the inflows. The NET present value deducts the ₹ 20,00,000 spent today.
Correct. The inflows are equal, so one multiplication suffices: 6,00,000 × 3.517231 = ₹ 21,10,338.76, less the outlay of ₹ 20,00,000, gives an NPV of ₹ 1,10,338.76.
This treats the inflows as arriving at the BEGINNING of each year, multiplying by a further 1.13. Cash flows are taken at the end of their year unless the question says otherwise.

questions.sourceRef: NPV with an annuity factor

questions.topic: Ch 4 · NPV of unequal inflows
questions.stem: The net present value of Machine B is:

options.explanation: This subtracts the outlay from the undiscounted inflows of ₹ 35,00,000.
This is the present value of the inflows before the outlay is deducted.
This applies the annuity factor 3.517231 to the average inflow of ₹ 7,00,000. An annuity factor is valid only when every flow is equal; here they are not.

questions.sourceRef: NPV with unequal flows discounted year by year

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Choosing between mutually exclusive projects
questions.stem: Only one machine can be installed. The company should choose:

options.text: Machine B, because its total cash inflows of ₹ 35,00,000 are the larger
options.explanation: Undiscounted totals ignore timing entirely. Machine B's larger inflows come later and cost ₹ 4,00,000 more to obtain.

options.text: Machine A, which has both the higher NPV (₹ 1,10,338.76 against ₹ 22,763.50) and the higher profitability index (1.0552 against 1.0095)
options.explanation: Correct. For mutually exclusive proposals the higher NPV decides, and here the profitability index points the same way: 21,10,338.76 ÷ 20,00,000 = 1.0552 for A, against 24,22,763.50 ÷ 24,00,000 = 1.0095 for B. Machine A adds more value from less capital.

options.text: Machine B, because its profitability index of 1.0095 is above zero
options.explanation: The profitability index test is 'above 1', not 'above zero'. An index of 1 means the project merely returns the required rate; anything at or below 1 is rejected.

options.text: Machine A on the profitability index, though Machine B is better on NPV
options.explanation: The premise is false here: Machine A wins on both measures. The two can disagree when outlays differ, but this is not such a case, so nothing needs reconciling.

questions.sourceRef: Mutually exclusive projects — the higher NPV decides

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Annuities · Case: building a fund and drawing it down
questions.case: Meera, an accountant in Pune, plans to set aside ₹ 1,20,000 at the end of every year for the next 20 years in a fund that earns 9% per annum compounded yearly. On the day the twentieth deposit is made she intends to move the whole accumulated sum into a safer scheme earning 7% per annum, from which she will draw 15 equal amounts, the first exactly one year later, leaving nothing at the end. Her adviser also asks her to consider depositing at the beginning of each year instead of the end. Work from unrounded factors and round only the final figures.

readLink.label: Read: Future value of an ordinary annuity, §9 →

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Accumulating the fund
questions.stem: The fund standing to Meera's credit on the day of the twentieth deposit is:

options.explanation: This adds the twenty deposits and credits no interest. Nineteen of the twenty deposits earn interest for at least a year.
This treats the deposits as made at the BEGINNING of each year, multiplying by a further 1.09. The question puts them at the end.
This uses the present value annuity factor 9.128546, valuing the deposits as at today rather than at the end of year 20.

questions.sourceRef: FV of an ordinary annuity

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Drawing the fund down
questions.stem: Each of the 15 yearly withdrawals from the 7% scheme will be:

options.explanation: This divides the fund by 15 and forgets that the undrawn balance keeps earning 7% throughout.
This divides by the FUTURE value annuity factor 25.129022. The fund exists at the start of the drawdown, so the present value factor is the right divisor.

Correct. P(15, 7%) = [1 − (1.07)^(−15)] ÷ 0.07 = 9.107914, so each withdrawal is 61,39,214.36 ÷ 9.107914 = ₹ 6,74,052.74. Fifteen such withdrawals total ₹ 1,01,10,791.04, the excess over the fund being the interest earned during the drawdown.
This assumes the withdrawals are taken at the beginning of each year, dividing further by 1.07. The first withdrawal comes a year after the switch, so this is an ordinary annuity.

questions.sourceRef: R = PV ÷ P(n, i)

questions.topic: Ch 4 · The effect of paying in advance
questions.stem: If Meera instead deposits ₹ 1,20,000 at the BEGINNING of each of the 20 years, the fund on the same date is:

options.explanation: Correct. An annuity due multiplies the ordinary annuity value by (1 + i): 61,39,214.36 × 1.09 = ₹ 66,91,743.65. The same ₹ 24,00,000 of deposits produces ₹ 5,52,529.29 more, purely because each deposit arrives a year earlier.
This is the ordinary annuity figure, unchanged. Shifting every deposit a year earlier must raise the fund.
This divides by 1.09 instead of multiplying. Paying earlier increases a future value; it never reduces it.
This applies the extra year's interest to the deposits alone (₹ 24,00,000 × 1.09) rather than to the accumulated fund.

questions.sourceRef: FV of an annuity due = ordinary annuity value × (1 + i)
